q: A shop sells 200 mugs at $8 each and its total costs are $1,200. What is its profit?
r: Revenue of $1,600 minus costs of $1,200.
w: $1,600, which is the total revenue before any of the costs of the business are subtracted
That is revenue, not profit.
$1,200, which is the total cost of running the shop for the period that was measured
That is cost, not profit.
$2,800, found by adding the revenue to the costs of the business for the same period
Revenue and cost are subtracted.

q: A bakery's fixed costs are $500 a month and each loaf costs $1 to make and sells for $3. How many loaves must it sell to break even?
r: 250 loaves
$500 divided by the $2 profit on each loaf.
w: 500 loaves, found by dividing the fixed costs by the cost of making a single loaf
The selling price matters too.
167 loaves, found by dividing the fixed costs by the selling price of a single loaf
The unit profit is price minus cost.
1,500 loaves, found by multiplying the fixed costs by the selling price of each loaf
Fixed costs are divided, not multiplied.

q: Which of these is a variable cost for a lawn-care company?
r: Fuel used to run the mowers
It rises with the number of lawns cut.
w: The monthly lease payment on the office where the company keeps its records
Rent does not change with output.
The yearly insurance premium paid on the company's trucks and equipment
Premiums are fixed.
The salary of the manager who runs the whole company all year round
A salary is fixed.

q: Which of these is a fixed cost for a restaurant?
r: The monthly rent on the building
It stays the same however many meals are sold.
w: The cost of the ingredients used in each of the meals that the kitchen prepares
Ingredients vary with meals.
The extra hourly wages of part-time staff hired for a busy weekend of heavy trade
Hours vary with demand.
The cost of the takeout boxes used for orders that customers take home each night
Boxes vary with orders.

q: A company's revenue is $90,000 and its expenses are $95,000. What does this show?
r: A loss of $5,000
Expenses are greater than revenue.
w: A profit of $5,000, because the larger figure is always the one that shows the profit
Profit needs revenue above expenses.
A profit of $185,000, found by adding the revenue and the expenses of the company
Revenue and expenses are not added.
Break-even, because the revenue and the expenses are close to each other in amount
Break-even needs them equal.

r: Sales minus the cost of the goods sold
It comes before operating expenses.
w: Sales minus all expenses of the business, including taxes and interest on loans
That is net profit.
The total amount of cash the business has in its bank account at the end of the year
That is a cash balance.
The cost of the goods the business bought from its suppliers during the year
That is cost of goods sold.

r: Revenue minus all expenses, including taxes and interest
It is the bottom line.
w: Revenue minus only the cost of the goods that were sold to customers during the period
That is gross profit.
The total revenue that the business earned from all of its customers during the year
That is revenue.
The amount of money that the owner takes from the business for personal use
That is owner's drawings.

q: A store buys a jacket for $40 and marks it up 50 percent. What is the selling price?
r: A 50 percent markup adds $20 to the cost.
w: $50, which adds only ten dollars to the cost, equal to a quarter of the original price
The markup is 50 percent of cost.
$90, which adds the full cost to the cost and then adds half of the cost again
The markup is only half of cost.
$20, which is the amount of the markup alone rather than the full selling price
Cost is added.

q: A business has revenue of $50,000 and net profit of $5,000. What is its profit margin?
r: 10 percent
w: 1 percent, found by moving the decimal one place too far when working out the percentage
The ratio is one tenth.
90 percent, found by dividing the expenses by the revenue and reading it as profit
That is the expense share.
45 percent, found by subtracting the profit from the revenue and dividing by the revenue
That is not margin.

q: If a business raises its price and sells fewer units, what must it check?
r: Whether total revenue and profit rose or fell
The price effect and the quantity effect work in opposite directions.
w: Nothing, because a higher price always means a higher profit whatever happens to sales
Fewer sales can offset it.
Nothing, because fewer units always means lower costs and therefore a bigger profit
Costs may not fall as much.
Only the number of units, because the price has no bearing on the revenue of the firm
Both matter.

q: What does the break-even point show?
r: The sales level where total revenue equals total costs
Profit is zero at that level.
w: The sales level at which the profit of the business is at its highest in a given year
That is maximum profit.
The sales level at which the business has no customers and earns no revenue
That is zero sales.
The sales level at which the business must close because it can no longer pay its staff
Not what the term means.

q: Why do businesses track their costs closely?
r: To set prices that cover costs and still earn a profit
Cost data guides pricing and spending.
w: To make the business look larger to banks than it actually is in terms of its sales
That would be misleading.
To avoid paying any tax on the profit that the business earns in each year
Tracking costs does not avoid tax.
To give the owner a reason to stop selling goods that customers want to buy
Not a purpose.

q: A firm's total cost rises from $10,000 to $12,000 when output rises from 1,000 to 1,500 units. What is the extra cost per added unit?
r: $2,000 divided by 500 extra units.
w: $10, found by dividing the original total cost by the number of units made at the start
That is average cost.
$8, found by dividing the new total cost by the number of units made at the end
That is average cost at the end.
$2, found by dividing the extra cost by the number of units made before the increase
The added units are 500.

q: Which action would most likely raise a company's profit?
r: Cutting costs without lowering the quality of its goods
Profit equals revenue minus costs.
w: Raising its costs while keeping the same prices and the same number of sales
That lowers profit.
Lowering its prices below its cost of making each unit of its goods
That causes a loss on each sale.
Spending money on a product that customers have shown no interest in buying
That wastes money.

r: Ongoing costs not tied to one product, such as rent and utilities
They are needed to run the business.
w: The cost of the raw materials used to make each product that the business sells
That is a direct cost.
The wages paid to workers who assemble each unit on the production line of the factory
That is direct labor.
The profit earned by the business after all of its costs have been paid out of revenue
That is profit.

q: A freelancer earns $3,000 in a month and spends $1,800 on costs. What is the profit?
w: $4,800, found by adding together the earnings and the costs for the month in question
Costs are subtracted.
$1,800, which is the amount spent on costs and not the profit that is left over
That is the cost.
$3,000, which is the earnings figure before any costs have been subtracted from it
That is revenue.

r: A product sold at a low price to attract customers
The store hopes they buy other items.
w: A product sold only to employees at a deep discount as a perk of working at the firm
Not the meaning.
A product that the firm makes at a loss and then hides from its customers entirely
Not the meaning.
A product that earns the highest profit of all the goods that the store sells
Opposite in this case.

q: Which is an example of an opportunity cost for a business owner?
r: The income given up by using a building for a shop instead of renting it out
It is the value of the next best use.
w: The price paid for the supplies used up in making goods during the month
That is an actual expense.
The wages paid to the staff for the hours they worked in the shop that week
That is an actual expense.
The tax that the business paid on its profits at the end of the year
That is an actual expense.

q: Why might a business lower a price on an item that is not selling?
r: To attract buyers and clear stock
Lower prices raise the quantity demanded.
w: To increase the profit on each unit, since lower prices always bring a higher margin
A lower price lowers the margin.
To show customers that the quality of the item has been lowered by the producer
Not the reason.
To stop customers from buying any items at all from the store for a while
Not the reason.

r: Limited resources to meet unlimited wants
It forces people to make choices.
w: A situation in which there are more resources than any person could ever want to use
The opposite.
A situation in which prices are set by the government for all goods and services
Not the meaning.
A situation in which everyone has all that they want without paying for any of it
Not the meaning.

r: The value of the next best alternative that is given up
Every choice has one.
w: The price a buyer pays for a product at the checkout counter of the store
That is the price.
The total amount of money a business spends on its supplies over a year
That is total cost.
The cost of an item after a discount has been taken off the price at the register
That is a sale price.

q: A student can work for $90 or study for an exam. What is the opportunity cost of studying?
r: The $90 the student gives up
It is the value of the best alternative.
w: Nothing, because studying is free and the student pays no money to take the exam
Time has a cost.
The grade the student will get on the exam if the studying goes well
That is a benefit.
The price of the textbook that the student already owns and has used before
That is a sunk cost.

q: What happens to the price of a good when demand rises and supply stays the same?
r: The price tends to rise
More buyers compete for the same amount.
w: The price tends to fall because more buyers lead to a larger amount for sale
Supply is unchanged.
The price stays the same because supply has not changed in the market for the good
Demand pushes the price up.
The price falls to zero because buyers have more power than sellers in the market
Not what happens.

q: What happens to the price of a good when supply rises and demand stays the same?
r: The price tends to fall
More goods chase the same number of buyers.
w: The price tends to rise because there is now a larger amount of the good for sale
More supply lowers price.
The price stays the same because demand has not changed in the market for the good
Supply pushes the price down.
The price rises to a record because sellers have more power than buyers in the market
Not what happens.

q: What is a surplus in a market?
r: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at a price
Sellers have unsold goods.
w: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at that price so that buyers cannot find goods
That is a shortage.
A situation in which the price of a good is exactly equal to its cost of production
Not the meaning.
A situation in which the government buys all of the goods that are offered for sale
Not the meaning.

q: What is a shortage in a market?
r: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a price
Buyers cannot find enough goods.
w: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at that price so that sellers have goods left
That is a surplus.
A situation in which a firm has more cash than it needs to pay its bills on time
Not the meaning.
A situation in which the government sets a limit on the price of a good for a year
Not the meaning.

q: What is the law of demand?
r: As price rises, quantity demanded falls, other things equal
Buyers purchase less at higher prices.
w: As price rises, quantity demanded rises too, since buyers think that high prices mean quality
The opposite.
As price rises, quantity supplied falls because sellers want to offer fewer of the goods
That confuses supply.
As price rises, the government must lower its taxes on the sale of the good
Not the law.

q: What is the law of supply?
r: As price rises, quantity supplied rises, other things equal
Sellers offer more at higher prices.
w: As price rises, quantity supplied falls because sellers prefer to keep the goods in stock
The opposite.
As price rises, quantity demanded rises because buyers want to pay a higher price
That confuses demand.
As price rises, the number of sellers in a market must stay the same for a long time
Not the law.

r: A good that can be used in place of another
If the price of one rises, demand for the other may rise.
w: A good that is used together with another good, such as a printer and its ink cartridges
That is a complement.
A good that is made from the waste left over by another product in a factory
Not the meaning.
A good that is sold only to businesses and never to ordinary customers in a store
Not the meaning.

r: A good used together with another good
If the price of one rises, demand for the other may fall.
w: A good that can be used in place of another good when the price of the first one rises
That is a substitute.
A good that is given away free to customers who buy a more expensive item
Not the meaning.
A good that has no value to customers and is never sold at any price by shops
Not the meaning.

r: A good whose demand rises as consumers' incomes rise
Most goods are of this type.
w: A good whose demand falls as consumers' incomes rise because they can afford something better
That is an inferior good.
A good that is bought by every consumer in exactly the same amount each year
Not the meaning.
A good that has no price because the government provides it to everybody for free
Not the meaning.

r: A market with one seller and no close substitutes
The seller has strong control over price.
w: A market with many sellers that each offer products that are almost the same to buyers
That is close to perfect competition.
A market with a few large sellers that watch each other's prices very closely
That is an oligopoly.
A market in which one buyer purchases all of the goods that many sellers offer
That is a monopsony.

r: A market dominated by a few large sellers
Each firm's actions affect the others.
w: A market with one seller and no close substitutes for the good that it makes and sells
That is a monopoly.
A market with thousands of small sellers that all offer exactly the same product
That is close to perfect competition.
A market in which the government sets the price of every good that is sold
That is a controlled market.

r: A general rise in prices over time
Each dollar buys less than before.
w: A general fall in prices over time that makes each dollar buy more than it did before
That is deflation.
A rise in the price of one good only while other prices stay the same
That is a relative price change.
A period in which output in the economy falls for several quarters in a row
That is a recession.

r: The total value of goods and services produced in a country in a period
It measures the size of an economy.
w: The total amount of money that the government holds in its accounts at the central bank
Not GDP in this case.
The total number of people who live in a country at a given point in time
That is population.
The total value of goods that a country sells to other countries in a year
That is exports.

q: What does the unemployment rate measure?
r: The share of the labor force that is jobless and looking for work
It excludes people not seeking work.
w: The share of all people in the country who have no job, including children and retirees
The base is the labor force.
The share of workers who earn the minimum wage out of all those who have a job
Not the measure.
The share of workers who work part time and would like to work more hours
That is underemployment.

r: A period of declining economic activity lasting several months
Output and jobs fall.
w: A period of rapid growth in output and jobs that lasts for several years in a row
That is an expansion.
A one-day fall in the prices of stocks on a major exchange in the country
Too short to be a recession.
A period in which prices rise sharply across all the goods that people buy
That is inflation.

q: What is the role of profit in a market economy?
r: It rewards firms that meet customers' needs and signals where to produce
Losses signal where to cut back.
w: It is set by the government for each firm so that no business earns too much money
Profits are not set by government.
It is paid out to workers only and never to the owners who started the business
Owners earn profit.
It has no effect on what firms choose to make or on how they use their resources
Profit guides decisions.

r: Focusing on producing a few goods or tasks
It raises output and efficiency.
w: Making every product in a single workshop so that one team does all of the work
That is the opposite.
Buying goods from many countries so as to offer buyers a wide choice of items
That is not specialization.
Selling a good at a price set by the government for every firm in the market
Not the meaning.

q: What is the circular flow model?
r: A model showing how money, goods and resources move between households and firms
Households sell resources and buy goods.
w: A model showing how prices rise in a spiral over time as wages and costs push each other up
That is a wage-price spiral.
A model showing the path that a delivery truck takes around a city each day
Not an economic model.
A model showing how a bank moves money between its branches in the same state
Not the meaning.

r: A tax on imported goods
It raises the price of foreign products.
w: A tax on exported goods paid by the seller who ships them to a foreign buyer
That is an export tax.
A payment made by the government to firms that sell goods in foreign countries
That is a subsidy.
A limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported in a given year
That is a quota.

r: A payment from the government to support a producer or activity
It lowers the producer's cost.
w: A tax the government charges on goods that are brought into the country from abroad
That is a tariff.
A fee the government charges for a license to run a business in the state
That is a license fee.
A fine the government charges to a business that breaks the rules of the market
That is a penalty.

r: A limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported
It restricts supply from abroad.
w: A tax on a good that comes into the country from abroad and is paid at the port
That is a tariff.
A payment from the government to a firm that sells its goods in foreign markets
That is a subsidy.
A rule that sets the lowest price at which a good may be sold within the country
That is a price floor.

q: In a market economy, who mainly decides what to produce?
r: Consumers and businesses through buying and selling
Prices guide the choices.
w: A central government plan drawn up by officials who set the output of each industry
That is a command economy.
Tradition, so that people follow the work of their parents and elders in all things
That is a traditional economy.
A committee of workers who vote on the products to be made once each year
Not how a market works.

r: The government makes most decisions about production and prices
Central planning decides what is made.
w: Individuals and firms make most decisions through markets, guided by prices and profit
That is a market economy.
Customs and habits passed down through generations decide who does what work
That is a traditional economy.
Private firms make all decisions while the government has no role of any kind
That is a pure market economy.

r: Customs and habits passed down through generations guide decisions
Roles are often set by family.
w: The government makes most decisions about production and prices for the whole economy
That is a command economy.
Prices and profit guide the decisions of firms and consumers in free markets
That is a market economy.
Firms and the government share decisions in a mix of markets and public rules
That is a mixed economy.

r: Private choice combined with government involvement
Most modern economies are of this type.
w: The government owns all firms and decides every price and output in the whole economy
That is a command economy.
Customs and habits decide all outcomes and there are no markets or government rules
That is a traditional economy.
All decisions are made by private firms and the state has no part in the economy
That is a pure market economy.

q: What is private property in a market economy?
r: The right of individuals and firms to own and use resources
It gives people an incentive to work and invest.
w: The right of the government to seize any asset at will without paying the owners
That would remove ownership.
The rule that all land and factories belong to the whole community and not to people
That is common ownership.
The rule that only wealthy families may own land and the machines that make goods
Not the meaning.

q: What is a key advantage of a market economy?
r: Prices and competition encourage efficiency and innovation
Firms respond to what consumers want.
w: A central plan removes all waste because one office decides what every person needs
That is a claim for command economies.
Everyone is guaranteed the same income whatever work they do or how hard they try
No guarantee exists.
The government sets the price of every good so that nobody can be charged too much
That is a controlled market.

q: What is a key disadvantage of a market economy?
r: Income inequality and little provision of public goods
Markets do not always protect everyone.
w: The government sets the price of every good, which leaves firms no freedom to compete
That is a command economy feature.
Customs decide who does each job, which limits the choices people can make in life
That is a traditional economy feature.
All firms are owned by the state and so there is no profit motive for the workers
That is a command economy feature.

q: What is a key disadvantage of a command economy?
r: Planners may misjudge what people want, leading to shortages and waste
Without prices, signals are weak.
w: Prices change so quickly that firms cannot plan and consumers cannot decide what to buy
That fits a market economy.
Customs prevent any change in methods, so progress is very slow across the generations
That fits a traditional economy.
Private firms earn too much profit and use it to take over the whole of the economy
Not a feature of command systems.

q: Which is an example of the government's role in a mixed economy?
r: Setting safety standards and providing public services
It corrects market failures.
w: Setting the price of every product sold in the shops and deciding who may buy it
That is a command economy.
Deciding which jobs each person must do according to the customs of the family
That is a traditional economy.
Taking no part in the economy and leaving all matters to private firms and buyers
That is a pure market economy.

r: An economic system based on private ownership and market competition
Capital is owned by individuals and firms.
w: An economic system in which the state owns the means of production and plans output
That is socialism or communism.
An economic system in which goods are shared equally by custom and tradition alone
That is a traditional system.
An economic system in which no one owns anything and all goods are free to take
Not an economic system.

r: A system in which the community or state owns major industries
It aims for more equal outcomes.
w: A system in which private firms own all industries and compete freely for customers
That is capitalism.
A system in which customs and family roles decide who does each type of work
That is a traditional economy.
A system in which there is no government and each person looks after himself
Not socialism.

r: Transferring a government-owned business to private owners
It moves activity from the public to the private sector.
w: The government taking over a private firm and running it as a public agency
That is nationalization.
A firm making its financial records secret from the public and from its regulators
Not the meaning.
A person keeping a personal diary that no one else is permitted to read at any time
Not the meaning.

r: The government taking ownership of a private industry
It moves activity from the private to the public sector.
w: Transferring a government-owned business to private owners through a public sale
That is privatization.
A firm moving its factories to a foreign country to take advantage of lower wages
That is offshoring.
A firm selling its goods in every region of the country at one national price
Not the meaning.

r: A good that people can use without paying and that one person's use does not reduce
National defense is an example.
w: A good that is sold in a store for a profit to anyone who is able to pay the price
That is a private good.
A good that is produced by a firm and sold only to the government at a fixed price
Not the meaning.
A good that is available only to people who live in the largest cities of the country
Not the meaning.

r: The part of the economy owned and run by the government
It includes schools and police.
w: The part of the economy owned and run by private individuals and firms for a profit
That is the private sector.
The part of the economy that is made up of charities that run on gifts only
That is the nonprofit sector.
The part of the economy that trades with other countries in goods and services
That is the foreign sector.

r: The part of the economy owned by individuals and companies
Firms there aim to earn a profit.
w: The part of the economy owned and run by the government to serve the public
That is the public sector.
The part of the economy made up of charities that rely on gifts from the public
That is the nonprofit sector.
The part of the economy that is kept secret from the government and the public
Not the meaning.

r: To protect consumers, workers and the environment
Rules correct failures that markets miss.
w: To make sure every business earns the same profit in each year of its operation
Not the aim.
To stop new firms from ever entering a market that already has large companies
Not the aim.
To raise the prices of all goods so that people buy fewer things from the shops
Not the aim.

r: A business that sells work or expertise instead of physical goods
A salon is an example.
w: A business that makes physical goods from raw materials and sells them to the public
That is a manufacturer.
A business that buys finished goods from producers and sells them to retail stores
That is a wholesaler.
A business that grows crops or raises animals for sale to food processors
That is an agricultural business.

r: A business that turns materials into finished goods
A furniture maker is an example.
w: A business that sells work or expertise to customers and does not make physical goods
That is a service business.
A business that buys finished goods and resells them to customers without changing them
That is a retailer.
A business that lends money to customers and earns interest on the loans it makes
That is a financial business.

r: A business that sells goods to the public
It is the last link in the channel.
w: A business that buys goods in bulk and sells them to stores and other businesses
That is a wholesaler.
A business that makes goods from raw materials in a factory and ships them to stores
That is a manufacturer.
A business that grows food on a farm and sells it to the makers of packaged goods
That is a producer.

r: A business that buys goods in bulk and sells them to retailers
It sits between the maker and the store.
w: A business that sells goods directly to the public from a store, website or catalog
That is a retailer.
A business that makes goods from raw materials and sells them under its own brand
That is a manufacturer.
A business that offers advice and expertise to clients for a fee rather than goods
That is a service business.

q: What is a producer of raw materials?
r: A business that grows or extracts basic materials
Farms and mines are examples.
w: A store that sells finished goods to the public from shelves in a shop or a mall
That is a retailer.
A factory that turns materials into finished goods ready for sale to stores
That is a manufacturer.
A business that lends money to other businesses so that they can buy materials
That is a financial business.

r: A business that handles money, such as a bank or insurer
It offers loans, savings and protection.
w: A business that makes cars and trucks in a plant and sells them through dealers
That is a manufacturer.
A business that sells groceries to the public from supermarkets in a town
That is a retailer.
A business that grows wheat and corn on a farm and sells it to mills
That is an agricultural business.

r: Buying and selling goods and services over the internet
It has no need of a physical store.
w: Selling only in physical stores where customers can see and touch the goods first
That is traditional retail.
Trading goods between countries by ship, rail and truck across the world's oceans
That is shipping.
Buying goods in bulk from a factory at a low price and storing them in a warehouse
That is wholesale buying.

r: Hiring another company to perform tasks or services
A firm might outsource payroll.
w: Doing all work inside the firm with its own employees and its own equipment
That is the opposite.
Selling goods to customers abroad by opening a branch office in a foreign country
That is exporting or expanding.
Moving a factory to another city at home to cut the cost of rent for the firm
That is relocation.

r: An organization that uses income to pursue a mission rather than pay owners
Surplus is reinvested.
w: An organization that loses money on purpose in order to give goods away to people
Not the meaning.
An organization that is owned by shareholders who receive its profits as dividends
That is a for-profit business.
An organization that is owned and run by the government to serve the public
That is a public agency.

r: A business owned and run by its members for their shared benefit
Members share in its profits or savings.
w: A business owned by a single person who keeps all of the profits for himself
That is a sole proprietorship.
A business owned by the government and run to provide a service at a low price
That is a public enterprise.
A business that competes with its members for the same customers in the market
Not the meaning.

r: Provides goods or materials to another business
It is a source of inputs.
w: Buys finished goods from stores and sells them to customers at a profit in a market
That is a retailer.
Competes with the firm for the same customers in the same market and region
That is a competitor.
Lends the firm money for a fixed period and charges interest on the loan made
That is a lender.

r: A business that uses another company's brand and system for a fee
The franchisee runs a local outlet.
w: A business that never charges fees and that earns all of its income from sales alone
Not the meaning.
A business that is owned by the government and run to serve the public at a low price
Not the meaning.
A business that sells only goods made by its own employees in a single workshop
Not the meaning.

r: The company that owns the brand and licenses it to others
It receives fees and royalties.
w: The person who buys the right to run a local outlet under the brand of a company
That is the franchisee.
The government agency that checks each franchise before it is allowed to open
Not the meaning.
The customer who buys goods from a franchise outlet in a shopping mall
Not the meaning.

q: What is the main purpose of a business?
r: To provide goods or services that meet needs and earn a profit
Customers' needs drive sales.
w: To give away goods and services to the public at no cost to any person who asks
That is a charity.
To avoid paying taxes by spending all income on the costs of running the firm
Not the aim.
To reduce the number of customers so that the owner has less work to do each day
Not the aim.

r: A business owned and run by one person
The owner is personally liable for debts.
w: A business owned by two or more people who share profits and unlimited liability
That is a partnership.
A business that is a legal entity separate from its owners and has shareholders
That is a corporation.
A business owned by its members and run for their shared benefit and use
That is a cooperative.

r: A business owned by two or more people who share profits and duties
General partners share unlimited liability.
w: A business owned and run by one person who keeps all of the profits for himself
That is a sole proprietorship.
A business owned by shareholders who elect directors to run it for them
That is a corporation.
A business owned by the government and run to serve the public at a low price
That is a public enterprise.

r: A business that is a legal entity separate from its owners
Shareholders have limited liability.
w: A business owned and run by one individual with no legal separation from the owner
That is a sole proprietorship.
A business owned by two or more people who share profits and unlimited liability
That is a partnership.
A business owned by the government with no shareholders and no profit motive
That is a public enterprise.

r: Owners are not personally responsible for debts beyond their investment
It protects personal assets.
w: Owners are fully responsible for all business debts, including those of the other partners
That is unlimited liability.
Owners may not be sued by anyone for any reason, no matter what the business does
Not the meaning.
Owners pay no taxes on the profits that they receive from the business each year
Not the meaning.

r: The owner is personally responsible for all business debts
Personal assets can be used to pay them.
w: Owners are not personally responsible for debts beyond the amount they invested
That is limited liability.
The owner has no responsibility for the debts of the business, which is a separate entity
That is limited liability.
The owner may borrow any amount of money without a lender checking the credit record
Not the meaning.

q: What is an advantage of a sole proprietorship?
r: It is simple to start and the owner makes all decisions
Few legal steps are required.
w: The owner is never personally responsible for any debts that the business may have
It has unlimited liability.
The business can raise large sums of money by selling shares to the public
That fits a corporation.
The business continues forever even if the owner dies or decides to retire
Continuity is limited.

q: What is a disadvantage of a sole proprietorship?
r: The owner has unlimited liability and limited ability to raise money
Personal assets are at risk.
w: The owner must share profits with a large number of shareholders each year
That fits a corporation.
The owner needs the approval of a board before making any decision for the firm
That fits a corporation.
The business pays corporate income tax and again taxes on the owner's dividends
That fits a corporation.

q: What is a disadvantage of a partnership?
r: Partners can disagree and may be liable for each other's acts
General partners share unlimited liability.
w: The business must be run by a single person who makes every decision for the others
That fits a sole proprietorship.
The business cannot add a new partner or raise money from any outside source
Partners can add capital.
The business pays corporate tax twice on all its profit before the partners are paid
That fits a corporation.

q: What is an advantage of a corporation?
r: Limited liability for owners and the ability to raise money by selling shares
It can also continue beyond its founders.
w: The owner makes all decisions alone and keeps all profits without sharing them
That fits a sole proprietorship.
The business is simple to start and needs no legal papers to be filed with the state
Incorporation requires filing.
The profits are never taxed at the level of the business or of the owners of shares
Profits are taxed.

r: The money needed to launch a business
It pays for equipment, inventory and early costs.
w: The profit earned by the business in the first year after it opens for trade
That is profit.
The money that customers pay to the business when they buy its goods or services
That is revenue.
The money that the owner takes out of the business for personal use each month
That is drawings.

q: Where might an entrepreneur get start-up funds?
r: Personal savings, loans, investors or crowdfunding
Each source has different costs.
w: Only from the government, since banks and investors never lend to new businesses
Many sources exist.
Only from customers, who must pay for all of the goods before they are made
Not the only source.
Only from a lottery prize that the owner wins in the year before starting the firm
Not a plan.

r: A written document describing a business's goals and how it will reach them
It is used to guide the firm and seek funding.
w: A list of the business's employees with their titles, pay rates and start dates
That is a staff list.
A report of the sales made by the business during the past twelve months of trade
That is a sales report.
A form that is filed with the state to register the name of a new business
That is a registration form.

q: What does the market analysis section of a business plan describe?
r: The industry, target market and competitors
It shows who the customers are.
w: The salaries of employees only, along with their job titles and the dates they started
That is staffing.
The legal structure of the business and the names of its owners and managers
That is the organization section.
The list of equipment that the business will buy with the money that it raises
That is a financial plan item.

r: A person who starts and runs a business and takes on its risk
Entrepreneurs seek profit.
w: A person who works for a fixed wage in a store and has no say in how it is run
That is an employee.
A person who lends money to a business and receives interest in return each year
That is a lender.
A person who buys goods from a business for his own use and does not resell them
That is a consumer.

q: Which is a risk that entrepreneurs face?
r: Losing the money they invested if the business fails
Income is not guaranteed.
w: Freedom from all legal responsibilities and from any need to pay taxes at all
Not a risk and not true.
A guaranteed profit every month, whatever the weather, the season or the economy
Profit is not guaranteed.
No competition ever, since new businesses have the market to themselves for years
Competition is normal.

r: Permission from the government to operate a business
Rules vary by place and type of business.
w: A guarantee of profit for the firm, issued by the government to licensed owners
No such guarantee exists.
A document that proves the business has paid all of its taxes for the year
That is a tax record.
A contract between the owner and a customer to buy goods at a fixed price
That is a sales contract.

r: A word, symbol or design that identifies a brand
It is legally protected.
w: The exclusive right to an invention granted by the patent office for twenty years
That is a patent.
The legal right to control copies of an original work such as a book or song
That is a copyright.
A secret recipe or process that a firm keeps from its competitors and its customers
That is a trade secret.

r: Exclusive rights to an invention for a set time
It stops others from copying it.
w: A word, symbol or design that identifies a brand and is protected by law
That is a trademark.
The legal right to control copies of an original work such as a book or song
That is a copyright.
A license to open a store, issued by the city to a retailer who wishes to sell goods
That is a business license.

r: The legal right to control copies of an original work
It covers books, music and art.
w: Exclusive rights to an invention for a set time granted by the patent office
That is a patent.
A word, symbol or design that identifies a brand and is protected by law
That is a trademark.
A guarantee of the quality of a work given by its author to the buyers of copies
Not the meaning.

q: What is a sole proprietor's main tax feature?
r: Business income is reported on the owner's personal tax return
There is no separate business income tax.
w: The business pays corporate tax and the owner pays tax again on any dividends received
That fits a corporation.
The business pays no tax of any kind on its profits and the owner pays none either
All income is taxable.
The business files a separate return and the owner is never taxed on a profit
Income passes to the owner.

r: Corporate profits taxed at the company and again as dividends
It affects C corporations.
w: Paying a tax twice on one purchase at the store, once at the register and once online
Not the meaning.
Filing two tax returns in one year, one for the state and one for the nation
Not the meaning.
Paying a tax on income and then paying the same tax again on the same income next year
Not the meaning.

r: A specific target you want to reach in your working life
It guides education and job choices.
w: A list of tasks done each day by an employee at the firm where he or she works
That is a to-do list.
A salary amount that the employer sets for you when you first start to work there
That is pay.
A rule that employees must follow while they are on duty at the workplace
That is a policy.

r: A group of jobs and industries with similar skills and interests
It helps students explore careers.
w: A group of employees at one office who share a floor, a manager and a coffee machine
Not the meaning.
A group of companies owned by the same person who runs them from a single building
Not the meaning.
A group of customers who buy the same product from a store at the same time
Not the meaning.

q: What is an interest inventory used for?
r: Identifying careers that match what you enjoy
It compares interests with job types.
w: Counting items in a warehouse by hand with a clipboard at the end of the year
That is a stock count.
Measuring how fast a worker can type or complete a task in a given time period
That is a skills test.
Listing the debts and assets of a person at the end of each financial year
That is a net worth statement.

q: Where can you find reliable information on job growth and pay?
r: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook
It is a government source.
w: An anonymous social media post that claims to know the facts about pay and jobs
Not reliable.
A friend's guess about what a job pays based on a story from the neighbor
Not reliable.
An advertisement placed by a company that is trying to hire as many workers as it can
May be biased.

r: Paid on-the-job training combined with classroom learning
It leads to a skilled trade.
w: A loan for starting a business, paid back over a number of years with interest
Not the meaning.
A permanent management role in a company, with a fixed salary and a company car
Not the meaning.
A short course taken in a classroom with no work experience and no pay for the student
Not the meaning.

r: Short-term work experience that helps you learn on the job
It may be paid or unpaid.
w: A permanent management role in a company with a fixed salary and a company car
Not the meaning.
A loan for starting a business, paid back over a number of years with interest
Not the meaning.
A course taken in a classroom in which students learn only from textbooks
Not the meaning.

r: A job that requires little or no prior experience
It is a starting point in a field.
w: A job that needs many years of prior experience and a senior title in the company
That is a senior role.
A job at the top of the company where the person manages all of the other staff
That is an executive role.
A job that pays the highest salary of any position in the whole of the firm
Not the meaning.

r: A skill useful across many jobs, such as communication
It carries over from one role to another.
w: A skill useful in only one job, such as running a single type of machine at a plant
Not transferable.
A skill that can be learned only by working for one particular employer for many years
Not transferable.
A skill that a person loses as soon as he or she changes employers or industries
Not transferable.

r: Continuing to learn new skills throughout your career
It keeps workers employable.
w: Learning only in high school, with the knowledge gained there lasting for the whole career
Not lifelong.
Learning only from books in a library or a classroom until a degree is earned
Not lifelong.
Avoiding new technology so that the old methods used by the firm can be kept
Not learning.

r: A personal ability such as communication or teamwork
It helps in all kinds of jobs.
w: A technical ability such as operating a particular machine or computer program
That is a hard skill.
A skill that can be measured only by a written examination set by an employer
Not the meaning.
A skill that applies to only one job and cannot be used in any other position
Not the meaning.

r: A specific, teachable ability such as using accounting software
It can be measured or tested.
w: A personal ability such as communication or teamwork that helps in many types of jobs
That is a soft skill.
A natural talent that cannot be improved by training or by any amount of practice
Not the meaning.
A habit of arriving on time and dressing neatly for work each day of the week
That is professionalism.

q: What is networking in career planning?
r: Building contacts who can share job leads and advice
Relationships open doors.
w: Setting up computers in an office so that staff can share files and printers
That is a computer network.
Waiting for employers to call after sending a single application by mail
Not networking.
Applying for many jobs at once without speaking to anyone at the firms
Not networking.

r: Following a worker on the job to learn what the work is like
It is a way to explore a career.
w: Taking over the job for a whole week while the regular worker stays away on leave
Not shadowing.
Replacing a worker permanently after a short period of watching the work
Not shadowing.
Working at night so that the day shift can leave earlier than normal at the firm
Not shadowing.

q: Why might someone choose a job with lower pay but stronger benefits?
r: Benefits like insurance and retirement matches add real value
Total compensation includes benefits.
w: Benefits are always worthless to workers who think about the long run of their careers
Not true in this case.
Benefits are paid only to workers who earn the highest salaries at the firm
Not true in this case.
Benefits reduce the number of hours that the employee needs to work each week
Not their purpose.

r: A periodic evaluation of an employee's work
It guides feedback and development.
w: A review of a product by a customer who has bought it and tried it at home
Not the meaning.
A list of the reasons why an employee should be given a higher salary
Not the meaning.
A plan for a company party which the managers organize each year for the staff
Not the meaning.

r: A summary of your education, skills and work experience
It is sent to employers.
w: A list of the company's products with their prices, sent to possible customers
Not the meaning.
A form that employers fill out to describe the duties of an open job
That is a job description.
A letter that thanks an interviewer for the time he gave to a candidate
That is a thank-you note.

r: Contact details, education, work experience and skills
It shows fit for the job.
w: A list of everything you dislike, along with a record of the jobs you have quit
Not relevant.
Your Social Security number, home address and the names of your parents on the page
Private data should not be listed.
A list of games you have played with scores and the teams that you have joined
Usually not relevant.

q: What is the main purpose of a cover letter?
r: To introduce yourself and show fit for the job
It highlights relevant strengths.
w: To list every job you ever had, with the dates, the pay and the names of your bosses
That is a résumé's role.
To complain about the way in which the company treats its present employees
Not its purpose.
To ask the employer for a higher salary than the one that the company posted
Not its purpose.

q: What should a student with no work experience include on a résumé?
r: School activities, volunteering and relevant skills
These show ability and character.
w: Invented job titles and made-up skills to make the application look impressive
Dishonest.
A list of games played, with scores and the teams that the student has played for
Not relevant.
Nothing at all, since employers do not hire people without any work history
Many hire first-time workers.

q: Why should you ask permission before listing someone as a reference?
r: So they are prepared and willing to speak well of you
They can be ready for a call.
w: So they can write your résumé for you and send it to the employers who are hiring
Not the reason.
Because it is required by law in every state before a name can be used on a form
Not required by law.
So they can be paid a fee by the employer for each call that they answer
Not paid in this case.

q: What is the best way to prepare for an interview?
r: Research the company and practice answers to common questions
Preparation builds confidence.
w: Wait to see what questions come up and answer them as best you can on the spot
Unprepared.
Learn nothing about the firm so that the interviewer sees how natural you are
Unprepared.
Memorize the pay of every worker at the firm to bring up during the interview
Not helpful.

q: How should you answer 'Tell me about yourself' in an interview?
r: Give a brief professional summary relevant to the job
Focus on skills and goals.
w: Share personal secrets about your family and friends with the interviewer
Too personal.
Recite your entire life story in detail, starting from your childhood years
Too long in this case.
Say you would rather not answer questions about yourself in the interview
Unhelpful.

q: Which is the best way to end a job interview?
r: Thank the interviewer and restate your interest
It leaves a positive final impression.
w: Ask only about vacation, pay and benefits so as to show that you are serious
Poor focus.
Walk out quickly without saying anything to the interviewer after the questions
Rude in this case.
Tell the interviewer that you have other offers and that you need an answer today
Pushy in this case.

q: What is a good next step after an interview?
r: Send a thank-you message
It shows appreciation and interest.
w: Post complaints about the company online if you do not hear back within a day
Unprofessional.
Call the interviewer every hour until you receive an answer about the job
Pushy in this case.
Wait silently for a year in case the employer decides to contact you again
Passive in this case.

q: What is a behavioral interview question?
r: A question asking about how you handled a past situation
It predicts future behavior.
w: A question asking what you would do in an imaginary case that has not happened
That is situational.
A question that asks only for your name and the date of your birth
Not behavioral.
A question about your plans for the weekend and your favorite sports
Not behavioral.

q: Which interview behavior is most professional?
r: Making eye contact and listening carefully
It shows respect and interest.
w: Checking your phone repeatedly while the interviewer is speaking to you about the job
Rude in this case.
Interrupting the interviewer so that you can make your own points more quickly
Rude in this case.
Arriving ten minutes late and apologizing only if the interviewer asks about it
Late in this case.

q: Which question is generally illegal for an interviewer to ask?
r: Whether you plan to have children
It could lead to discrimination.
w: Why you want this job and what skills you would bring to the position
Allowed in this case.
What your career goals are for the next five years in the industry
Allowed in this case.
Whether you can work the hours that the job requires, including weekends
Allowed in this case.

r: A form that gives an employer information about you
It lists history and contact details.
w: A contract that guarantees a job to the person who signs it and returns the form
Not a guarantee.
A list of company products with their prices, sent to potential customers
Not the meaning.
A bill from an employer for the cost of hiring a new member of staff
Not the meaning.

q: Where can you look for job openings?
r: Job boards, company websites and personal contacts
Several sources work together.
w: Nowhere, since jobs are secret and are filled by the employers without any notice
Jobs are posted.
Only in the newspaper from a century ago that is kept in the local library
Outdated in this case.
Only through ads that say you will earn a fortune without doing any real work
Often scams.

q: What should you do when you decide to leave a job?
r: Give proper notice and leave on good terms
It protects references.
w: Take company property as a souvenir of your time at the firm before you leave
Theft in this case.
Stop coming to work without telling anyone at the firm where you have gone
Unprofessional.
Tell your coworkers that the company is a bad place to work as you depart
Unprofessional.

q: What is a notice of resignation?
r: A message telling an employer you are leaving the job
It is usually given in advance.
w: A message offering you a job, sent by an employer after the interview has been held
That is a job offer.
A message from an employer telling you that your employment has been ended
That is a termination notice.
A message from a coworker asking you to join a new club at the workplace
Not the meaning.

r: A formal proposal from an employer to hire you under stated terms
It lists pay and conditions.
w: A request from you to leave a job, which you hand to your manager in a letter
That is a resignation.
A list of open jobs posted on a website by a firm that is hiring staff
That is a job posting.
An invitation to attend an interview at the office of the company next week
That is an interview invitation.

r: Discussing pay and benefits with an employer before accepting
Research helps you ask for a fair amount.
w: Demanding a high salary without research into what other firms pay for the work
Unprepared.
Accepting the first offer without asking any questions about pay or benefits
Not negotiation.
Refusing to talk about pay at any time during the hiring process at the firm
Not negotiation.

q: Why do employers conduct background checks?
r: To verify information and reduce hiring risks
They confirm claims on applications.
w: To lower employee pay by finding faults in the history of the applicants
Not the reason.
To discover which applicants have the most friends on social media sites
Not the reason.
To find reasons for refusing to hire any worker who applies to the firm
Not the reason.

r: Behaving responsibly, respectfully and reliably at work
It includes punctuality and courtesy.
w: Dressing carelessly in all cases, because the quality of the work is all that matters
Not the meaning.
Arriving late without notice and leaving as soon as the work for the day is done
Not the meaning.
Arguing with supervisors about every decision they make so as to show independence
Not the meaning.

q: What is the best response to praise at work?
r: Say thank you and share credit with others who helped
It shows humility.
w: Brag about it to everyone in the office to show your worth to the company
Boastful in this case.
Ignore the praise and walk away without saying a word to the person
Rude in this case.
Say that the praise is not deserved and that the team did all of the work
Self-deprecating.
